title: How laughter works.
body:
Different comedians can arrive at similar comic moves by entirely different routes. An ordinary assumption becomes absurd when taken literally. A small irritation grows into a catastrophe. A sentence leads us one way, then turns against itself.

This constellation is a way to explore those relationships—not a ranking of the funniest people, nor a genealogy of who influenced whom.

title: Requirements Are Design Work
body:
A team watches someone repeat the same edit across 200 records. The requirement becomes: “Add bulk editing.”

But that's a proposed solution, not yet a justified requirement.

The person needs to make the intended changes accurately, without affecting other records, and with less repetitive effort. Bulk editing might accomplish that. So might a reusable rule, an import, or a different workflow that eliminates the repetition.

The distinction matters because requirements shape which solutions we consider. **How we frame the problem shapes which requirements we consider necessary.**

Too often, teams collect feature requests, call them requirements, and hand them to builders. They specify too much, distinguish too little, and mistake the length of the list for the quality of the thinking.

Good requirements follow from an understanding of the situation, a judgment about what should improve, and the conditions a solution must respect. Each should have a reason: a need to satisfy, an outcome to achieve, or a constraint to honor. Different designs may satisfy the same requirements. Some may make the original problem disappear.

This isn't merely documentation. It's design work. It requires understanding causes, deciding what matters, considering alternatives, making trade-offs, and testing whether the chosen design produces the intended change. Following a proposed design through real situations can reveal missing requirements, unintended consequences, and better ways to solve the problem.

A product can satisfy every stated requirement and still fail. Sometimes the implementation is wrong. Sometimes the requirements were. Sometimes the team chose the wrong problem.

Two related articles develop the reasoning: [Uncovering the Causes of Demand](https://mattlane66.github.io/articles/uncovering-the-causes-of-demand/) examines how we understand the situation and identify opportunities. [Design as Functions](https://mattlane66.github.io/articles/design-as-functions/) examines how we derive requirements, evaluate candidate designs, and test whether they work.

**The point isn't to write more requirements. It's to make better judgments about what must be true, and why.**

title: Shaping Is Finding a Buildable Path
body:
A team reaches the middle of a project and discovers that a simple interface change needs a new permission model. It looks like an engineering delay. But the costly question was there before anyone started building.

Shaping is the work between deciding an opportunity matters and committing a team to build. It turns a rough idea into a coherent, buildable solution path without creating the finished design or code.

Begin with a **frame**: where people struggle, what they do today, what happens as a result, and what they want to be different. Then set an **appetite**: the amount of team time the opportunity is worth, often two to six weeks. The appetite is a budget to design within, not a prediction of how long an unlimited solution will take.

Bring together people who understand the user, the design, and the system. A shaping session is not a status meeting, a brainstorming exercise, or a spec review. It is a few hours of working on the same problem, making and discarding provisional ideas, and deciding what belongs together.

1. **Lay out the parts.** Put the important screens, states, actions, rules, and constraints on a shared board. Some will not have a place yet.

2. **Find different paths.** Connect those parts into two or three plausible ways the product could work. Use an interaction schematic to show the screens or states, the actions people can take, and what changes when they act. This exposes the whole interaction before anyone worries about pixels.

3. **Bring the system into view.** Under the visible actions, name the permissions, data, functions, and services they depend on. A button labeled “Share” might require a new access rule, an invitation record, and a notification. This is where engineering knowledge reveals what an innocent-looking interface conceals.

4. **Sketch and investigate selectively.** If the arrangement of elements matters, draw a rough focal sketch of that part—not a finished mockup of every screen. If a technical, design, legal, or performance question could change the path, run a small spike and return with what you learned.

5. **Check the fit.** Compare the paths against the original struggle, desired outcome, appetite, cost, complexity, risks, and existing system. Identify what fits, what is weak, and what blocks a path. Move between the whole design and its troublesome details until the trade-offs are clear.

The point is not to remove every unknown. It is to find a way the parts can work together, expose the expensive surprises before implementation, and leave capable builders room to make the remaining decisions.

Stop when the team can explain the path, what is in and out, why it fits the appetite, which risks have been resolved, and where implementation still has latitude.

Then package the result in an Input Design Document so people who were not in the room can understand the same concept and build it without constant direction.

Put the method to work in the [Shaping Board](https://mattlane66.github.io/planning-skills-for-agents-and-humans/shaping-board/), or use the [Figma playing field template](https://www.figma.com/community/file/1490786031847199566/shaping-session-playing-field-copy-me-template) for a collaborative shaping session.

**The document records the shaping. It does not do the shaping.**

title: Progress isn't always getting closer to where you intended to go.
body: Progress isn't always getting closer to where you intended to go. Sometimes it's discovering somewhere better to go. Never make your next decision merely because it was part of your previous plan. Make it because, given what you now know, it's still the best decision.

title: The Beauty of Fit
body:
A thing can be simple and still fail, or complex and work beautifully. What matters is how its parts fit together and how the whole serves its purpose.

There are two dimensions to this fitness. Structural fit: the parts form a coherent whole. Functional fit: the whole suits what it is meant to do. When the two reinforce each other, we may experience that coherence as beauty.

Abstract reasoning helps us discover and create this fit. It allows us to look beyond a thing's existing form, identify the relationships that matter, and imagine how they might be arranged differently.

Sometimes the breakthrough isn't a better part, but a better relationship between parts.

Beauty may reveal fitness, but it cannot prove it. What appears coherent must still work in reality.

title: The questions I keep returning to
body:
The questions I keep returning to in my work never change:

**How do we perceive what matters, discover the relationships that govern it, decide what ought to exist, give that judgment a working form, and recognize when reality proves us wrong?**

title: When to articulate. When to scan.
body:
Some things are easier to describe than to find. Others are easier to recognize than to describe.

Reordering groceries may take one sentence. Choosing a chair may require seeing twenty. Reviewing an agent's changes may require a visual comparison of what existed before and what exists now.

The mistake is to assume that conversation should replace the graphical interface. Conversation reduces the effort of navigation but introduces the effort of articulation. Which is easier depends on what the person knows, what the task requires, and what remains uncertain.

An agent can do the work without making every judgment for us. We may need to explore before we can specify a goal, delegate steps we don't know how to perform, or inspect a result before we can accept it.

The design problem is not choosing between conversation and graphical interfaces. It is making the next judgment easier.

Let people articulate what is easier to say, scan what is easier to recognize, delegate what is easier to execute on their behalf, and inspect what they need to judge.

title: The Art of Seeing
body:
Someone glances toward the door. We notice the glance. We infer impatience. We may be wrong.

The art of seeing is learning to distinguish what we observe from what we make of it. We cannot know reality directly, but we can improve our ability to notice what matters, interpret what we notice, and recognize when we are mistaken.

We must become observationists.

Four abilities we can cultivate

Attention — What am I noticing, and what am I missing?

Learn to direct attention deliberately. What stands out is not necessarily what matters.

Discrimination — What differences can I detect?

Learn to perceive distinctions you once missed. A musician develops an ear for subtle changes in timing, tension, and harmony.

Interpretation — What might explain what I observe?

Look for patterns, relationships, and causes. Keep what you observe distinct from what you think it means. An explanation is not an observation.

Calibration — What would show me that I'm wrong?

Test your interpretations against independent evidence. Notice when expectations fail. Revise your understanding when the evidence demands it.

It is not enough to think differently. We must learn to see differently.

title: Shape Up’s appetite is a value judgment, not an estimate.
summary: Shape Up’s appetite is a value judgment, not an estimate.
body:
Shape Up’s appetite is a value judgment, not an estimate: decide how much team time a problem is worth, then shape scope to fit that creative constraint.

Agents keep that principle, but now you have to budget machine execution and human review separately.

Before the work starts, set:
• Appetite: what the problem is worth in person-weeks
• Machine cap: that appetite in agent-hours, using today’s production factor
• Quality floor: what must be true for the result to count

Example: a 2-person, 6-week appetite = 12 person-weeks = 480 human-equivalent hours.

At a 2× production factor, the machine cap is 240 agent-hours. At a 25% review rate, using the full cap implies about 120 hours of actual human review—not 480 hours of human production.
Then shape scope and execution to fit.

Clear the quality floor with the least human review. Spend more agent time—or add scope—only when the expected gain justifies the extra work and review.

As the machine cap approaches, cut optional work, verify what matters, preserve state, and land.

At the cap, stop. Raising it is a new bet.

Human-equivalent team time is the durable unit. Production factor and review rate are exchange rates for today’s agents. Update them from actual runs.

title: Opportunity Judgment Loop
body:
Opportunity Judgment Loop

1. Sense — notice a signal in the world.
Look for anomalies, workarounds/misfits, unmet needs, changing behavior, or new capabilities that make previously impossible things possible. Treat need-signals and capability-signals differently: a new capability is an opportunity hypothesis, not evidence of demand.

1.1. Immerse — experience the problem directly.
Do the work yourself where possible. Observe, shadow, trace, handle the artifacts, and encounter the real constraints. Move from hearing about the problem to knowing its world.

2. Internalize — build your own model of what is really happening.
Understand the underlying forces well enough to explain why things work as they do, distinguish causes from symptoms, and anticipate what happens next. Map the incentives that sustain the current reality. Question inherited assumptions rather than taking the existing system as given.

2.1. Form a point of view — make a judgment about what ought to exist.
Use your understanding of what is, together with your values, taste, imagination, and sense of possibility, to choose a better future worth pursuing. This is a judgment, not a conclusion forced by the evidence.

3. Test — put that conviction back into the world.
State what you expect to happen and what evidence would change your mind. Then create the smallest artifact, prototype, experience, or intervention that lets reality respond. Prefer real behavior over stated agreement.

4. Calibrate — learn from the gap between prediction and reality.
Compare what you expected with what actually happened. Record the prediction, result, and lesson so the learning survives the moment and improves future judgment.

Sense → Immerse → Internalize → Form a Point of View → Test → Calibrate

World → Self → World

Outside-in provides the signal.
Immersion turns signal into understanding.
Judgment turns understanding into conviction.
Testing turns conviction back into evidence.
Calibration improves the next judgment.

The goal is earned conviction: a strong view of what ought to exist, grounded in reality but not constrained by its current form.
Ultimately, it's about opportunity authorship, i.e., deciding which futures deserve to exist.

title: Product judgment is the learned ability to make good decisions under ambiguity.
summary: Product judgment is the learned ability to make good decisions under ambiguity.
body:
Product judgment is the learned ability to make good decisions under ambiguity about what software should do, for whom, how simply it can do it, and whether the resulting artifact is actually good.
In the agentic era, that matters even more. When AI agents handle more of the implementation, the scarce skill is no longer simply writing the code.

Software outcomes depend partly on implementation capability and partly on product judgment. A capability is more differentiating insofar as differences in that capability account for a larger share of differences in outcomes across comparable teams. If AI compresses cross-team differences in implementation capability more than it compresses differences in product judgment, without increasing the relative causal importance of implementation enough to offset that compression, then product judgment will become relatively more differentiating. To the extent AI produces those conditions, product judgment is becoming a more important differentiating human capability in software development.

title: High-value questions to ask when scoping which opportunities and desired outcomes to prioritize:
summary: High-value questions to ask when scoping which opportunities and desired outcomes to prioritize:
body:
High-value questions to ask when scoping which opportunities and desired outcomes to prioritize:

Is this a proven behavior or a new one?
How large is the opportunity, and at what rate is it growing?
What are the baseline outcomes today?
What assumptions are we making?
Does this problem/opportunity recur?
What happens if we do nothing?
Why does it matter now?
How much time is it worth spending on this problem?

Prioritize problems by their expected user and business value. Prioritize solutions based on how well they fit the problem, context, and constraints.

title: Intent–Discover–Align–Execute Method
body:
Intent–Discover–Align–Execute Method

Begin with intent, not commands. Explain the outcome you want, your current understanding, and the relevant context.

Ask the gen AI model/LLM interface to challenge the framing, surface assumptions and unknowns, identify blind spots, and explore alternative approaches. Use that feedback to establish a shared understanding of the goal, constraints, success criteria, and initial plan or task.

Then execute. Continue identifying and resolving new unknowns as they emerge, revising the plan when the evidence suggests a better path.

Intent → Discovery → Alignment → Execution ↺ = higher-quality human-AI computer interactions and results.

Dictation, rather than typing and then reading the results aloud, is generally the better tool to use when engaging with this method. It allows you to access partially formed thoughts more effectively, match the speed of your thinking, engage the phonological loop, and evaluate your logic more quickly.

title: Distribution should not sit outside the product as a later marketing problem.
summary: Distribution should not sit outside the product as a later marketing problem.
body:
Distribution should not sit outside the product as a later marketing problem. It has to be designed into the first use and proven from the beginning. The moment a user gets value, the product should naturally create something worth sharing, inviting others into, or building on. Otherwise, the company is not running a strategy; it is running a hope strategy.
The FTUX should create the first turn of the flywheel: a user gets value, produces a shareable object, brings someone else in, and that next person’s participation makes the object more valuable.

title: Coding is the production of software.
summary: Coding is the production of software.
body:
Coding is the production of software.
Product is the ongoing selection, shaping, coordination, and evolution of software under changing conditions.

That is why “build” has two meanings.
Sometimes you build to learn.
Sometimes you build for quality, reliability, and scale.

title: A director is a navigator who has learned to leave the first-person view without abandoning what the first-person view knows.
summary: A director is a navigator who has learned to leave the first-person view without abandoning what the first-person view knows.
body:
A director is a navigator who has learned to leave the first-person view without abandoning what the first-person view knows.

The navigator encounters the system from inside it. Friction is not theoretical there. A beautiful design can still be frustrating. A coherent strategy can fall apart in use. A feature can work and still feel heavy in the hand.

The director works at another scale. They step outside the immediate experience long enough to see relationships the navigator cannot: sequence, context, boundaries, emphasis, consequence. They turn what happens locally into a structure that can be shaped deliberately.
The two roles want different things.

The director wants coherence across the whole.
The navigator wants momentum through the next moment.
The director asks: Where are we going, and why does this belong?
The navigator asks: Can I do what I need to do from here?
Neither question is sufficient.

The director’s edge is not doing more of the work. It is knowing what to ask for. The broader their knowledge, the more possibilities they can see—and the better their questions become.
But questions eventually meet the floor.

Stay only on the balcony and the system becomes elegant but lifeless. Stay only on the floor and every local irritation can become the whole problem.

There is another reason to keep returning to the navigator’s position: people do things with systems that their designers never anticipated. They find shortcuts, workarounds, exploits, and new uses. They reveal possibilities that cannot be discovered from the diagram because they emerge only through use.

So the relationship is not director over navigator.
It is a loop:
Navigate → notice → step out → reframe → reshape → navigate again.

They descend until they can feel the friction.
They ascend until they can see what the friction means.
Then they change the frame and go back down.

title: One way to understand taste is to notice its absence.
summary: One way to understand taste is to notice its absence.
body:
You lack taste when you can tell something is off but cannot say precisely what, why it matters, or what you would change. You reach for another perspective because you do not yet trust your own judgment.

Taste closes that gap.

It is the ability to perceive meaningful differences, understand the choices producing them, know the standards and context those choices operate within, and judge which tradeoffs best serve the thing being made.

Good taste is not certainty or preference. It is disciplined discrimination: knowing what matters, what does not, what belongs, what gets in the way, and why.

And it remains accountable to reality. You make the choice deliberately, compare it against alternatives, observe what it actually does, and revise your judgment when the effect is not the one you intended.

Taste is preference that has learned to explain itself, reproduce itself, and correct itself.
